The image is referenced as Figure 3-1 in section 3.2, which describes the operator station as the area where an operator receives parcels from the tippers. The photograph visually identifies seven key components: the tipper, chute, stacklight, plastic curtain, operator station HMI, push-buttons, and rotary station. This view is useful for understanding the physical layout and component placement within the station, aiding in troubleshooting, maintenance, and operator training.

This artifact is a photograph of the rotary station, a mechanical assembly positioned beneath the chute in the OptiSweep system. The station is equipped with bag racks designed to hold parcel bags and can be rotated to allow an operator to access additional bags for manual replenishment. The image highlights the physical layout of the station, including the central foot brake mechanism. The accompanying text warns of a pinch point hazard between the chute and the station during rotation and specifies that the foot brake must be engaged while bags are being filled and disengaged before rotating the station.

This artifact is a photograph of the operator station push-button panel from the OptiSweep Operation and Maintenance Manual. It illustrates the physical controls used to initiate tipper cycles. The panel includes buttons for starting the standard left and right tipper cycles, as well as dedicated buttons for handling Surepost totes. A prominent emergency stop button is also shown, which is described in the nearby text as being reserved for situations involving imminent danger to personnel or equipment damage. The accompanying table clarifies that the tipper will ignore a tip command if no tote is gripped, and the corresponding button will flash only when a tote is present.

This artifact is a labeled maintenance diagram (Figure 3-4) from the OptiSweep Operation and Maintenance Manual, page 27, section 3.2.3. It depicts the left tipper assembly, which receives totes from AGVs and empties parcels into a chute. The diagram identifies 14 key components, including the Z-axis and A-axis motors, hard stops, cable carriers, counterbalances, timing belt, CLINK controller cover, air valve connection junction box, and gripper. The accompanying text notes that left and right tippers are identical but assembled as mirror images. This artifact is useful for identifying parts during troubleshooting, maintenance, or replacement procedures.

The system directs parcels from the sorter into totes. When a tote reaches a customer-specified weight, parcel count, or volume, the WCS signals the sorter PLC to stop diverting. An AGV retrieves the full tote and another AGV places an empty tote. The WCS then signals the sorter PLC to resume sorting. QR codes on the floor direct the AGV to an open tipper. The tipper's gripper pulls the tote onto the tipper, which deposits the parcel into a bag via a chute. A bagging employee generates and places a bag ID label, then places the bag on a take-away conveyor. After tipping, the WCS indicates task completion, and the AGV removes the empty tote and re-enters the sorter area for further commands. In case of mis-sort, bad tip, or tote overload, the WCS directs the AGV to the right side of the hospital station for operator handling. The AGV then moves to the left side to pick up an empty tote and re-enters the sorter area.
Geek+ is the manufacturer of the AGVs. The specific model used is the Geek+ P40 (V2.0).

It triggers AGVs to retrieve full totes and place empty ones. It directs AGVs to open tippers or the hospital station based on operational status. It also signals AGVs when a tipping cycle is complete.

A DATA RESET button is available to zero all data.

The Process Status indicators are green when the condition is true. The system's automated operation is managed by the WCS. Operators only need to interact manually with the system at the tipper and hospital stations. The provided procedures in the manual apply specifically to these two station types.

The system startup procedure is initiated from the system HMI. The operator must first navigate to the 'system API screen' and then press the 'SYSTEM STARTUP' button. This is a manual step to begin system operation.
The 'system API screen' is a navigable screen on the OptiSweep system HMI. Its confirmed function is to provide the SYSTEM STARTUP control. It is a critical interface for system operation.
The startup procedure requires two preconditions: 1) AGVs must be powered on (refer to P40A V2.0 user manual for AGV startup instructions), and 2) the main disconnect must be in the ON position.

During operator station startup, a flashing ESTOP indicates a fault condition. The operator must physically pull out the ESTOP button and then press the RESET button on the HMI screen to clear the fault state before proceeding.

The left tipper has axes Z1 and A1; the right tipper has axes Z2 and A2. Pressing AUTO REF initiates homing for each axis. During homing, the axis button changes from green to yellow to indicate movement. The tipper motor moves until it senses the home proximity switch, then stops.

Once all axes are homed, the operator presses CYCLE START. This command moves the tipper motor from the home position (where it stopped after homing) to a ready position, preparing the tipper for automatic operation.
After the tipper reaches the ready position, the operator places it in AUTO mode. In AUTO mode, the tipper waits for the Warehouse Control System (WCS) to send instructions for automated operation.
The operator station is stopped by pressing the CYCLE STOP button located on the operator station main screen. This is distinct from the system-level shutdown procedure described in section 5.2.

The documented step to stop the operator station is a single action: pressing the CYCLE STOP button on the operator station main screen. This is distinct from the system shutdown procedure, which is initiated from the system HMI API screen.

The startup procedure for the operator station includes: 1) Verifying AGVs are powered on. 2) Verifying the main disconnect is ON. 3) At the operator station control panel, if the E-STOP is flashing, pulling out the E-STOP and pressing RESET on the HMI to clear faults. 4) Homing every axis (Z1, A1, Z2, A2) by pressing AUTO REF; the axis button changes from green to yellow while moving and stops when the home proximity switch is sensed. 5) Pressing CYCLE START to move the motor from home to ready. 6) Placing the tipper in AUTO mode to wait for WCS instructions.

The system should be shut down between sorts to allow AGVs to charge. The procedure is: 1) On the system HMI, navigate to the system API screen. 2) Press SYSTEM SHUTDOWN. 3) The AGVs go to a shutdown queue.

The operator station main screen includes a CYCLE STOP button. This button is the primary control for stopping the operator station, as per the documented procedure. An image of this screen is available in the manual.

Jogging mode allows manual positioning of the left and right tipper end effectors. It is accessed from the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen (F3) on the operator station HMI. The automatic tipping cycle must be stopped by pressing CYCLE STOP before jogging is enabled. Pressing JOG opens the jogging screen. The Z1 and A1 axes control the left tipper; Z2 and A2 axes control the right tipper. The + button moves the Z-axis up and rotates the A-axis towards the operator. The – button moves the Z-axis down and rotates the A-axis away from the operator. Pushing an axis to a hard stop will register a fault.

The jogging screen is accessed by pressing the JOG button on the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen (F3) after a CYCLE STOP. It provides manual mode controls for four axes: Z1 (left tipper vertical), A1 (left tipper rotation), Z2 (right tipper vertical), and A2 (right tipper rotation). Each axis has + and – buttons for movement.

When manually jogging the tipper axes (Z1, Z2, A1, A2), if an operator pushes an axis until it hits a physical hard stop, the axis will register a fault. This is a known condition during manual operation.

Section 5.7 of the manual details recovery processes for non-recoverable faults. An example of such a fault is a motor overload fault on a tipper, which may occur while a tote is clamped by the gripper.

If a non-recoverable fault such as a motor overload occurs on a tipper, the operator must navigate to the 'MCP_Dual' screen (F3) on the operator station HMI and press CYCLE STOP to halt the tipping cycle.
The 'MCP_Dual' screen is a specific HMI screen on the operator station. It is referenced in the context of stopping a tipping cycle during a non-recoverable motor fault recovery process.

The CYCLE STOP control is a button on the operator station HMI, specifically mentioned in the context of the 'MCP_Dual' screen. Its function is to stop the tipping cycle, which is a required step when recovering from a non-recoverable motor fault on a tipper.

This fault type cannot be recovered via software. An example scenario is a motor overload fault on a tipper while a tote is clamped by the gripper. The recovery process uses the MCP_Dual screen (F3) on the operator station HMI. The operator must press CYCLE STOP, then JOG to enter manual mode. If any axes show a fault, press RESET. If the tote is lifted off the robot, jog the Z-axis or A-axis to position the tote on or nearly on the robot. Use A1 and Z1 for the left axis; use A2 and Z2 for the right tipper. Then press AUTO to enter automatic mode, press CYCLE START to release the grippers and command the robot to the hospital station, and finally press RESET after the robot has left the tipper.

The MCP_Dual screen is accessed by navigating to F3 on the operator station HMI. It is used during non-recoverable fault recovery processes. The screen displays axis statuses for Z1, Z2, A1, and A2, and includes buttons for CYCLE STOP, JOG, RESET, AUTO, and CYCLE START. It also shows a 'Manual Mode' indicator and a 'Fault' indicator when applicable.

During a non-recoverable fault recovery, if a tote is lifted off the robot, the operator can jog the Z-axis or A-axis to position the tote on or nearly on the robot. The manual specifies that A1 and Z1 are used for the left axis, and A2 and Z2 are used for the right tipper. The axis statuses and controls are displayed on the MCP_Dual screen (F3).

During the final steps of a non-recoverable fault recovery for operator station motors, after pressing AUTO and CYCLE START, the grippers release and the robot is commanded to go to the hospital station. The operator must press RESET after the robot has left the tipper.

This fault is verified on the operator station HMI. The OUT Fault Status for the affected tipper should have a value of 82. Recovery involves forcing a value on OUT W1: a value of 3 if the tote and AGV are ready to continue, or 32771 if the AGV needs to go to the hospital.

After verifying the AGV stuck fault (OUT Fault Status 82), the operator forces a value on OUT W1. Enter 3 if the tote and AGV are ready to continue working. Enter 32771 if the AGV needs to go to the hospital. The forced value is applied by checking the adjacent box, waiting 10 seconds, and then unchecking it.

This information is required for safe and effective manual fault recovery when Geek+ cannot recover the AGV automatically. The operator must know the Robot ID, the fault description from RMS, the bin/tote status, and the empty AGV status for the zone if the AGV is under a rack.

The manual references the 'szonestaging' state as a required condition during fault recovery. In the 'Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV' procedure, the operator must verify the AGV status is 'szonestaging' on the HMI. If the AGV is moving to the Hospital instead, it must be removed and re-added. The 'AGVS Lost Tasks' procedure also requires AGVs to be in the 'szonestaging' state before restarting the system.

This procedure addresses the scenario where empty AGVs have lost their tasks due to an RMS restart. Steps include: 1) E-stop RMS. 2) Remove and re-add AGVs without totes twice using Tote API Controls. 3) If the system needs to be restarted, ensure AGVs are in the 'szonestaging' state (verified on HMI). 4) Press E-stop again. 5) Resume RMS. A note indicates that best practice is to shut down and restart to ensure synchronization.

The manual references 'Tote API Controls' on page 26 as the mechanism to add an AGV to a zone or to remove and re-add AGVs during fault recovery. It is used in both the 'Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV' and 'AGVS Lost Tasks' procedures.

During the 'Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV' procedure, after adding an AGV, the operator must verify its status is 'szonestaging'. If the AGV is instead moving to the 'Hospital', the procedure requires the operator to remove the AGV and add it again.

During the 'Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV' procedure, after adding the AGV in RMS, the operator must wait for the AGV to turn blue. This indicates a successful transition before verifying the 'szonestaging' state.

The recovery concept for a 'Faulted AGV with Tote' involves a sequence of actions: E-stop the RMS, remove the AGV from the RMS, take the tote to the Hospital and remove the AGV via the Hospital HMI, add the AGV back into the RMS, press the E-Stop again, and resume the RMS. This process references other sections for specific steps like AGV API Controls and Add/Remove AGV.

For an 'AGV Fault During Exchange', the described concept is to E-stop the RMS, remove the faulted AGV that is lifted. If the AGV behind it does not backfill, that AGV should also be removed. The final step is to introduce a new tote at that location and place an empty AGV in that zone.

The recovery concept for 'AGV Lost Tote No Fault' includes: E-stop the RMS, press the brake release on the AGV, push the AGV to the Hospital, remove and re-add the AGV at the Hospital station PC, power cycle the AGV, roll it over a QR code when lights are green, locate the missing tote and bring it to the Hospital for removal, and finally add the tote back into the system so the AGV can take it to the sorter.

The Hospital station PC is referenced as the interface for removing and adding AGVs during recovery scenarios, such as when an AGV has lost a tote. The operator is instructed to use this PC to remove the AGV and then add it back into the system.

The manual mentions an AGV brake release in the context of recovering an AGV that has lost a tote. The operator is instructed to press the brake release on the AGV to then push it over to the Hospital.

If the AGV behind the faulted one does not backfill, remove that AGV as well. 4. Introduce a new tote at the location and place an empty AGV in that zone.
After an AGV is power cycled and its lights turn green during the 'AGV Lost Tote No Fault' recovery, the operator must roll the AGV over the QR code in front of the Inbound Hospital Station.

After an AGV is power cycled (turned off and on), its lights will turn green to indicate it is ready. The operator must then roll the AGV over the QR code in front of the Inbound Hospital Station. This status is part of the 'AGV Lost Tote No Fault' recovery procedure.

The Zebra scanner is a versatile hand-held device used at both the hospital and the sorter. At the sorter, it is used for managing totes during manual operations, including tote replacement, maintenance, repair, and handling damaged totes.

It is essential that a tote manually removed from the sorter stand is returned to its original position with the same Tote ID. Failure to do so will require rescanning to properly associate the tote with its designated location. Proper scanning ensures the system recognizes the correct placement and avoids operational errors.

The manual explicitly lists the use cases for the Zebra scanner at the sorter: tote replacement, maintenance, repair, and handling damaged totes. These are distinct from its use at the hospital station for adding and removing totes.

When an obstruction or dropped parcel is on the floor, the corrective action is to reference the E-stop zone map, press E-STOP for the appropriate zone, remove the parcel/debris, pull the E-STOP, press the blue RESET button, and the system will resume operation.

When an AGV is motionless on the floor due to a fault, the corrective action is to locate the faulted AGV (possibly referencing RMS for the error), reference the E-stop zone map, press E-STOP for the appropriate zone, remove the faulted AGV, pull the E-STOP, press the blue RESET button, and the system will resume operation.

If too many AGVs are being directed to the hospital, the cause may be a tipper fault or upstream issues. For a tipper fault, look for a fault beacon on the operator station, correct the fault, and return the tipper to service. For upstream issues, check each tipper for totes sent to the hospital. If at least five totes have been continuously sent, push E-STOP, call a supervisor, and investigate the reason.

An air line clog in the pneumatic system is possibly caused by debris in the small ports inside the valve. The correction is to use compressed air to clean out the ports. If contamination is common, a better filtration system may be needed.
For issues related to the Geek+ P40 (V2.0) robots, reference the P40A (V2.0) user manual, Document version: V1.1 (20231206). For any sortation related issues, refer to the DSC Support hotline.

The operator station is a component of the OptiSweep system. Daily preventive maintenance tasks are: 1) Inspect the controller for damage. 2) Verify stacklights are operational. 3) Ensure the chute is free of debris (e.g., stuck labels).

The hospital station is a component of the OptiSweep system. Daily preventive maintenance tasks for each hospital station are: 1) Verify the barcode scanner is operational. 2) Verify the stacklight is operational. 3) Ensure the tabletop is free of debris.

The OptiSweep system includes P40 (V2.0) robots and a tipper. Maintenance procedures for the robots are documented in the P40A (V2.0) user manual, Document version V1.1 (20231206). Maintenance for the tipper is handled by Lifecycle Performance Services (LPS), reachable at 888-444-4647.
The operator station must be inspected daily for: damage to the controller, operational stacklights, and a chute free of debris (e.g., stuck labels).
Each hospital station must be inspected daily for: an operational barcode scanner, an operational stacklight, and a tabletop free of debris.

For maintenance related to P40 (V2.0) robots, reference the P40A (V2.0) user manual (Document version: V1.1, 20231206). For maintenance related to the tipper, contact Lifecycle Performance Services (LPS) at 888-444-4647.

The operator station is part of the daily preventive maintenance routine. The inspection checklist includes: (1) checking the controller for any damage, (2) confirming that the stacklights are operational, and (3) ensuring the chute is free of debris, specifically noting stuck labels as an example.

The daily preventive maintenance procedure explicitly calls out checking the chute for debris and provides 'stuck labels' as a specific example. This indicates that label jams or accumulation in the chute are a recognized operational concern for the operator station.
During daily preventive maintenance, each hospital station must be inspected to ensure the barcode scanner is operational, the stacklight is operational, and the tabletop is free of debris.

Once the system is live, tipper inspections must be done weekly for the first four weeks. Then, inspections must occur monthly for four months. Then, inspections must occur every 6 months going forward. The Tipper Inspection Checklist on page 209 should be used during inspections.

Visually inspect both Z-axis linear rails for wetness of grease and/or signs of dried grease. If the rails are dry (not wet with grease), lubricate the bearing blocks using automotive bearing grease (e.g., Mobil1). There are two bearing blocks with one standard 1/4-in. nipple on each end each, so there are four nipples to grease. Adding 1.0 to 3.0 cc of grease to each block should be adequate. Wiping grease on the rails is not adequate.
The manual references a Tipper Inspection Checklist located on page 209. This checklist should be used during inspections to avoid missing important tasks.

The checklist includes the following tasks: Inspect the Operator Station controller for damage; Ensure Operator Station chute is free of debris; Verify stacklights are operational; Inspect the guards and verify attaching hardware is secure; Inspect all QR codes on the floor for damage or peeling; Inspect all QR codes on the racks for damage or peeling.

A tipper needs to be re-commissioned after any part is replaced. No further details on the re-commissioning procedure are provided in this section.

The automatic referencing procedure involves pressing RESET, then AUTO REF to reference all tipper axes. The 'R' icons turn green upon completion. After referencing, press AUTO and then CYCLE START to restart operation.

To manually reference axes, navigate to the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen (F3) on the operator station HMI and press CYCLE STOP to stop the automatic tipping cycle. This allows manual positioning of the end effector.
The stacklight is a three-segment assembly. Replacement involves disconnecting an M12 connector. Required PPE includes safety glasses and gloves. The procedure is estimated to take 30 minutes.
The stacklight is connected via an M12 connector. Disconnecting this connector is the first step in the removal procedure.

The tipper is mounted to a sub-plate with four hex head screws. It has connections for power (6-pin Molex), Ethernet (to ClearLink controller), and an air line with a quick disconnect at the bottom of the column. A side panel provides access to the motor. Removal of the gripper and counter-balance weights is optional but recommended before removing the tipper.

The power cable uses a 6-pin Molex connector. The Ethernet cable connects to the ClearLink controller. The air line has a quick disconnect located at the bottom of the column; during removal, the quick disconnect is left on the tipper side. All three connections are routed through a conduit to the column.

The tipper mounts onto an existing sub-plate. Four hex head screws hold the tipper to the sub-plate. A side panel secured by nine self-tapping screws can be removed with a 3/8-inch wrench or socket to access the motor.

Before removing the tipper, LOTO must be applied to the tipper (referencing Operator Station Lockout/Tagout procedure on page 2). Required PPE includes safety glasses and gloves. The procedure recommends optionally removing the gripper (page 97) and counter-balance weights (page 95) to facilitate the replacement.

The tipper commissioning process is required after any tipper component replacement. The goal is to align the replaced tipper with the other tipper, ensuring grippers and axes are level. The process requires two people, three hours, and tools including a level, digital measure, large square, and screwdriver. The 12-step outline covers power-up, controller parameters, IP address, I/O check, end effector plumbing, Z-axis homing, leveling, motor clearance, tote pickup/dump positions, firmware loading, and validation.
The documented requirements for performing tipper commissioning are: two personnel, an estimated time of three hours, and tools including a level, digital measure, large square, and screwdriver.

The 'Visu_MDs' screen is an HMI screen on the operator station. It is accessed by pressing F2. Its documented use is for setting initial parameters for each axis of the tippers. Changing settings on this screen requires maintenance or admin level login.
As part of the tipper commissioning process (step 9), the tote pickup position must be set to a specific value of 16 3/4 inches.

The setup procedure requires a Windows 10 or 11 laptop with 'Barcode Interface.exe' installed, a Zebra DS3608-SR scanner dock with USB cable and power adapter, two 120 VAC outlets, and network connectivity from the laptop to the AGV and Hospital control (validated by ping). The scanner must be charged until the red battery symbol turns green. The user must log into the laptop with a FORTNA account, launch the Barcode Interface application, check connectivity (green indicator), and if red, click 'Calibrate Scanner'. Settings are accessed via a settings button with the default password 'Opti'. Prefixes must be verified against labels on totes and locations. The HTTP and OPC URLs must be changed to contain the AGV control and Hospital control IP addresses respectively, and saved with the 'Save Settings' button.

The application is identified by a FORTNA logo on the desktop. It provides connectivity status (green/red indicator) and a 'Calibrate Scanner' function for troubleshooting. It has a settings area, protected by the default password 'Opti', where prefixes for totes and locations are verified, and HTTP and OPC URLs are configured to point to the AGV control and Hospital control IP addresses. Settings are saved via a 'Save Settings' button.

The laptop used for scanner setup must be able to reach the AGV and Hospital control over the network. This is a prerequisite validated by a ping command. The Barcode Interface application also provides a visual connectivity status (green for good, red for bad) on the bottom right of its screen. If the status is red, the user must click 'Calibrate Scanner' and follow onscreen instructions. The HTTP and OPC settings within the application must then be configured with the respective IP addresses of the AGV control and Hospital control.

The setup uses a Zebra DS3608-SR scanner dock. The connection procedure involves connecting the RJ45 side of the USB cable to the back of the dock, the USB end to the laptop, and the auxiliary power connector to the power adapter, which must be plugged into a 120 VAC outlet. The dock should light up when powered. If the scanner battery is depleted, indicated by a red battery symbol on top of the scanner, it must remain on the dock to charge until the symbol turns green.
When configuring a replacement scanner, the user must click the settings button in the Barcode Interface application and supply a password. The source states the default password is 'Opti'.
